sources.title: Samuel Slater (Q442104), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-06): label 'Samuel Slater', description 'English-American industrialist', Korean label 새뮤얼 슬레이터, born 9 June 1768, died 21 April 1835 (a second value of 20 April is also recorded), citizenship United States and United Kingdom. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

National Park Service, Lowell National Historical Park, 'Early American Manufacturing' (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Slater rose from apprentice to overseer in an English factory using the Arkwright system, left England disguised as a farmer, and in December 1790, working for mill owner Moses Brown, started up the first permanent American cotton-spinning mill in Pawtucket, mechanizing carding and spinning with a workforce of nine children aged 7 to 12; a generation of millwrights and workers trained under him spread mills across New England, and the 'Rhode Island System' of small rural spinning mills set the tone of early industrialization for two decades; the mill had over 100 workers by 1800. Federal park-service history, favourable but notes the child workforce.

National Park Service, Blackstone River Valley National Historical Park, 'Samuel Slater' (read in full). Fifth son of a Belper farmer, trained in Jedediah Strutt's water-powered mill, left England secretly at 21, reached Pawtucket where Almy and Brown's attempts to run a mill had failed and had the first working water-powered textile mill a year later; created the 'Rhode Island System' using the whole family as workers, most noted for child labour (children 7 to 12 were the first employees); with his brother John built Slatersville, described as America's first planned industrial community; kept building and financing mill villages across southern New England until his death in April 1835. Park-service biography.

National Park Service, Blackstone River Valley National Historical Park, 'Slater Mill' (read in full). Brown hired Slater in December 1789; Slater judged Brown's machines would not work and for several years worked with local mechanics such as the Wilkinson family to make new ones, getting them running in December 1790; he hired children who were paid for hours under his supervision, and in mill villages child workers aged 8 to 14 earned steady wages but lived 'under the constant control and manipulation of their employers'; the 1793 Almy, Brown and Slater mill is the Slater Mill. CRITICAL-CONTEXT passage on labour. Park-service site page.

Talya Housman, 'Slater Mill and Rhode Island System', Rhode Island Historical Society EnCompass essay (read in full): quotes Slater's letter of 2 December 1789 to Moses Brown ('a few days ago I was informed that you wanted a manager of cotton spinning'), Brown's reply that 'we are destitute of a person acquainted with water-frame spinning', the first batch of yarn on 20 December 1790, Slater's division of the process into steps by age and gender, hiring whole families and building a town with a company store (Slatersville completed 1807, over 300 people by 1810) and the spread of the system. Educational essay by a Brown University doctoral candidate; the letter quotations are from White's 1836 Memoir.

Rhode Island Historical Society manuscripts finding aid, 'Almy & Brown Records' (MSS 029; chronology read). Gives the dated business record: letters in December 1789, Slater's arrival in January 1790, the firm 'Almy, Brown & Slater' organized 5 April 1790 with Slater in control of manufacturing and Almy & Brown as marketing and purchasing agents, the sources' disagreement on whether he altered old machinery or built new, the 1793 mill, his brother John joining in 1806 to build the Smithfield mills that became Slatersville, and the 1832 dissolution. Archival finding-aid chronology compiled by the archive.

Nell Porter Brown, 'Tracing America's Industrial Roots in the Blackstone River Valley', Harvard Magazine, May-June 2020 (read in full; interview with the Old Slater Mill Association director). Slater, after seven years in a state-of-the-art English mill from age 14, brought a sense of the machinery's systematic coordination; he told no one, not even his mother, that he was leaving, so he is 'Slater the traitor' in England and 'the father of American manufactures' here; with Moses Brown, the machinist David Wilkinson and woodworker Sylvanus Brown the group built the first successful water-powered cotton-spinning machine; the 1793 mill opened with nine employees under 12, a practice described as common in English factories; and in 1797 he built the White Mill across the river with Wilkinson, pumping out thread continuously, 'the system Slater envisioned', splitting from Almy and Brown. Magazine feature quoting a museum director.

PBS, 'Who Made America? Innovators: Samuel Slater' (read in full). Slater divided factory work into steps so simple that children could do it; left England in 1789 covertly and, backed by Moses Brown, built the first water-powered cotton-spinning mill in America; Slatersville in 1803 with tenement houses and a company store; the 'Rhode Island System'; the page defends child labour as normal for its time. Popular-history broadcaster page, favourable.

James L. Conrad Jr., 'The Making of a Hero: Samuel Slater and the Arkwright Frames', Rhode Island History 45(1), February 1986, article beginning on p. 3 (scholarly article; the opening argument read from the Rhode Island Historical Society's scan, pages 3-12). COUNTER-VOICE: argues that the traditional story that Slater built the Arkwright machinery alone and from memory is a heroic construction traced to Moses Brown's 1791 letter and George S. White's 1836 Memoir; the firm's business records show local artisans (Oziel Wilkinson, Sylvanus Brown and others) worked on the old frames and that yarn was spun on Arkwright frames two months after his arrival, so Slater received more help and needed less time than believed; it also notes intense hostility between Almy and Slater from 1829 and that White omitted Almy's initial reluctance to endorse the story. Scan OCR was noisy; the argument is clear but quotations are not reproduced.

'Slater, Samuel', in The Biographical Cyclopedia of Representative Men of Rhode Island (Providence: National Biographical Publishing Co., 1881; Internet Archive scan, entry read). SELF-REPORT-DERIVED AND EULOGISTIC: narrates his emigration, the December 1789 letter exchange, the 1790 partnership, his second partnership with his father-in-law's family and the mill across the river, his move to the Webster area (Slater & Tiffany), his 1822 inspection of Amoskeag Falls and his 1829 financial losses; follows White's 1836 Memoir (the heroic account Conrad questions), so it is not an independent check and is used only for dated business moves.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_slater_nps_lowell, src_slater_rihs_essay, src_slater_harvard | 1789-1790 | park-service history, historical-society essay, magazine feature] He recognized that American states and merchants wanted British spinning technology that Britain would not export, left England in 1789 with his Arkwright-system experience, and wrote to Moses Brown after hearing he needed a manager. The pattern is documented; the claim that he read Britain's industry as overextended is a museum director's interpretation and no source quotes him on his reasons, and the sources are all favourable. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.55 to 66 / 0.50 because the 'saw the opening' reading rests on a museum director's interpretation and uniformly favourable sources.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_slater_nps_lowell, src_slater_blrv_person, src_slater_harvard, src_slater_pbs | 1789 | park-service histories, magazine feature, broadcaster page] He left England in 1789 in breach of British restrictions on emigration by skilled textile workers, disguised as a farmer and telling no one, to start a mill in a country with no textile industry. Several independent institutions give the same facts; his motives are not quoted, and the same act made him 'Slater the traitor' to the British, so the impact is dual-edged. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): risk_tolerance lowered from 68 / 0.55 to 64 / 0.5 because the disguised-departure story is part of the heroic tradition that the scholarly source challenges.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_slater_rihs_essay, src_slater_rihs_almy, src_slater_blrv_mill | December 1789 | historical-society essay quoting his letter, finding aid, park-service page] On hearing that Moses Brown wanted a manager of cotton spinning he wrote to offer his services on 2 December 1789, then travelled to Pawtucket, judged Brown's machines would not work and proposed making new ones. The letter exchange is dated in the archive record and quoted in the essay; the quotation reaches us through White's Memoir, and his later work is partly credited to local mechanics. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): proactive_agency lowered from 68 / 0.55 to 64 / 0.5 because the offer-letter account comes largely from park and museum pages repeating one tradition.

systems_abstraction.rationale: [src_slater_harvard, src_slater_pbs, src_slater_rihs_essay, src_slater_conrad | 1790-1797 | magazine feature, broadcaster page, historical-society essay, scholarly article] Sources credit him with grasping how the Arkwright machines and the division of labour fit together (work divided into simple steps by age and gender; a continuous-production mill from 1797). But Arkwright had already divided labour, the 'systematic coordination' remark is a museum director's, and Conrad shows the heroic technical credit was inflated. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.45 to 56 / 0.38 because the evidence for his personal conceptual contribution comes from popular summaries and a heroic tradition that the scholarly source challenges.

collaboration.rationale: [src_slater_blrv_mill, src_slater_harvard, src_slater_rihs_almy, src_slater_conrad | 1790-1832 | park-service page, magazine feature, finding aid, scholarly article] He relied on local mechanics such as the Wilkinson family and Sylvanus Brown, worked in the Almy, Brown and Slater partnership from 1790 to 1832, and built later mills with relatives and his brother John; against that, he left the Almy partnership for his own mill in 1797 and Conrad reports intense hostility between Almy and Slater from 1829. A real pattern of partnerships with documented friction, hence a modest score and a dual-edged impact.

portrait.source: Steel-plate portrait engraving of Samuel Slater, imprinted 'Van Slyck & Co. Boston' with a facsimile signature 'Samuel Slater', published as a plate in The Biographical Cyclopedia of Representative Men of Rhode Island (Providence: National Biographical Publishing Co., 1881); scan from the Internet Archive copy (Brigham Young University, Harold B. Lee Library), plate leaf 46. The page scan (2200 x 2979) was cropped to the oval portrait with its imprint and signature (1240 x 1860) and downscaled to 800 x 1200 with no upscaling. The Rhode Island Historical Society's 1986 article reproduces the same plate with the caption 'Samuel Slater, 1768-1835' from the same book (RIHS Collection).
portrait.license: Public domain: a US book published in Providence in 1881 (Internet Archive metadata: date 1881); a pre-1931 US publication, and the engraving was made about 46 years after the sitter's death
portrait.attribution: Van Slyck & Co., Boston, steel engraving in The Biographical Cyclopedia of Representative Men of Rhode Island, 1881, via the Internet Archive
portrait.creator: Van Slyck & Co., Boston (engraver)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (alt-dependent) (lead) / CONFIRMED, LEAD USED. The lead's plate in the 1881 Biographical Cyclopedia of Representative Men of Rhode Island was found, opened and read: it is a steel engraving imprinted 'Van Slyck & Co. Boston' with a facsimile signature 'Samuel Slater' (leaf 46 of the Internet Archive scan). HOLDER RECORD CHECKED: Internet Archive metadata for biographicalcycl00prov (date 1881, Providence, National Biographical Publishing Co., BYU Harold B. Lee Library scan; no rights field set, so no restriction found but also no explicit PD statement: the rights basis is the documented 1881 US publication, a pre-1931 US publication). The RIHS journal article (Conrad 1986, source read) reproduces a Slater plate captioned as taken from this book, p. 35, held in the RIHS Collection. INSCRIPTION CHECK: I looked at the full-size page; plate shows a bust of a man in a dark coat and white stock with the imprint and a signature 'Samuel Slater'. The adjacent plate in the same book (leaf 54) is signed 'John Slater' and shows a different man (a brother or relative), so I explicitly confirmed I had the right one; no contradiction. KIND: historical_depiction (a book engraving made 46 years after his death, probably after an earlier likeness not identified by the book; so it is not documented as a sitting). The unsourced Commons file Samuel-Slater.jpg was not used. Crop: oval portrait, imprint and signature from the 2200x2979 page scan (1240x1860) downscaled to 800x1200, never upscaled; saved as public/portraits/samuel-slater-van-slyck-1881.jpg. REGION north_america (career base: Pawtucket, Rhode Island, and New England from 1790; English-born, citizenship shown as United States and United Kingdom; follows the career-base precedent such as Domeyko). ERA 19th_century (precedent Eli Whitney b. 1765). Nationality codes US and GB. ZERO POLITICS: portfolio building; the US government bounties are context, and no politics, diplomacy or industrial espionage as a legal matter is scored. His business conduct is scored only as business: the child-labour workforce of the Rhode Island System is documented by the park-service pages and is context for the dual-edged impacts, with no inference about his motives, character or private life. No family or health inference. VOCABULARY: occupation entrepreneur only (inventor was not used because Conrad shows the machinery credit is contested), field business only, impact domains entrepreneurial, industrial and innovation, tags founder and organizer, archetype entrepreneurial_builder; all present in the repo and in en.ts and ko.ts. KO NAME: 새뮤얼 슬레이터 is the Korean Wikidata label (Q442104). HISTORICAL ATTRIBUTION (lead screen: attributable): CONFIRMED (attribution_confirmed true), with the caveat that the heroic account of his technical feat is contested by scholarship, so technical-creativity rows are not scored. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: National Park Service, Lowell National Historical Park, 'Early American Manufacturing' (https://www.nps.gov/lowe/photosmultimedia/early_american.htm). READ (9 substantive sources plus Wikidata): (1) NPS Lowell; (2) NPS Blackstone River Valley 'Samuel Slater'; (3) NPS Blackstone 'Slater Mill'; (4) RIHS EnCompass essay by Housman; (5) RIHS Almy & Brown records finding aid (chronology); (6) Harvard Magazine feature (2020); (7) PBS Who Made America; (8) Conrad, 'The Making of a Hero' (Rhode Island History 1986; pages 3-12 read from a noisy scan); (9) the 1881 Biographical Cyclopedia entry. PERSPECTIVES: federal park-service histories, a state historical society (essay and archive), a magazine feature quoting a museum director, a broadcaster page, a critical scholarly article and an 1881 eulogistic compendium. COUNTER-VOICES AND LIMITS: Conrad argues the 'built it alone from memory' story is a heroic construction (Brown's 1791 letter and White's 1836 Memoir) and that local mechanics and the old frames mattered; the NPS Slater Mill page says child workers lived under constant control and manipulation; the 1881 entry and the PBS page are admiring and derive from White. DATE CONFLICTS: the first mill started up in December 1790 (several sources) while the finding aid places the partnership in April 1790 and the 1881 text prints April 1790 after the December 1790 start; the cards use December 1790 for start-up only. NOT OPENED: White's 1836 Memoir itself, Tucker's 1984 book and the Business History Review article, the Urban History Review review (bot-walled), Smithsonian Magazine (read but not used), Encyclopedia.com Gale entry (read in part; contains errors such as 'power looms', not used). EXCLUSIONS: 'father of the American factory system' labels as fact, the claim he worked entirely from memory, politics and bounties, his family, health and wealth at death, the 1829 losses (single eulogistic source), and all 'first' wording except where a source I read states it.
